claims.text: A 1–2 wt% Ni coating can be applied uniformly to W particles by chemical solution deposition below 400 °C.
Spark-plasma sintering the Ni-coated W–Cu material at approximately 1200 °C will form an in situ transient Ni–Cu alloy layer at W–Cu interfaces.
The transient Ni–Cu phase will spread along W particle surfaces during sintering.
An interfacial coating or reaction layer can improve wettability and metallurgical bonding between particles and a metal matrix.
The Ni–Cu interlayer will act as a graded interlayer that promotes strong W–Cu metallurgical bonding.
The interfacial layer will fill microvoids at W–Cu interfaces.
The interfacial layer will reduce interfacial energy differences.
The Ni coating and resulting interlayer will reduce phase separation and make the W–Cu structure more uniform.
Ni-coated W–Cu consolidated by spark-plasma sintering will have a significantly lower void fraction than an otherwise identical composite made with bare W particles.
More continuous W–Cu interfacial contact will enhance thermal transport relative to unmodified spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu.
The Ni-coated composite will have improved mechanical durability relative to unmodified spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu.
The defect-minimized Ni-modified W–Cu interface will remain mechanically robust under fusion-relevant irradiation.
Conventional spark-plasma sintering of bare W particles in Cu typically suffers from phase separation and void formation that impair thermal transport and mechanical integrity.
Sintering at approximately 1200 °C with controlled pressure and dwell time can enable transient liquid formation without excessive formation of brittle intermetallic phases.
Excessive Ni coating thickness or overreaction could produce enough brittle intermetallic phase to reduce mechanical toughness.
The magnitude of the performance gains depends on optimizing Ni coating thickness and the sintering profile.
